parsed.hook: Margaret River’s gravelly loam doesn’t just grow Cabernet—it grows Cabernet with a savory edge. Howard Park’s Leston blend layers 10% Syrah into the mix, a nod to the region’s ability to balance ripeness with peppery tension. This isn’t just another Aussie Cab; it’s a wine that drinks like a cooler-climate red with warm-climate generosity.
parsed.wine_summary: Howard Park’s Leston Cabernet Sauvignon is a Margaret River classic that punches above its weight. The producer, founded in 1986, was one of the first to prove that Western Australia could rival Bordeaux in structure and complexity. The 2016 vintage—14.5% ABV, pH 3.7, and 6.1 g/L TA—shows why: it’s ripe but not jammy, with the acidity to keep dark fruit in check. The Syrah addition (10%) isn’t just a gimmick; it amplifies the wine’s savory, peppery notes, a signature of Margaret River’s maritime-influenced climate. This is a wine that straddles the line between New and Old World, offering the accessibility of Australian Shiraz with the restraint of a Left Bank Bordeaux.
parsed.terroir_expression: Margaret River’s soils are a mix of red gravelly loam, loamy gravel over clay, and deep infertile sand—all underpinned by Forest Grove ironstone. These free-draining soils stress the vines just enough to concentrate flavors without overripening, while the region’s Mediterranean climate (warm days, cool maritime nights) preserves acidity. The result? Cabernet with blackcurrant depth and a Syrah-driven peppery lift, all framed by the ironstone’s mineral grip. The wine’s 14.5% alcohol doesn’t feel hot because the tannins and acidity are in sync—a hallmark of Margaret River’s ability to balance power and finesse.
parsed.vinification_summary: Howard Park ferments this wine in stainless steel to preserve fruit purity, then ages it in French oak (30% new) for 12–14 months. The oak is subtle, adding spice without overpowering the wine’s natural savory character. The Syrah is co-fermented with the Cabernet, a technique that integrates the two varieties seamlessly. Cold soak (pre-fermentation maceration at low temperatures) extracts color and aroma without harsh tannins, while malolactic fermentation in barrel softens the acidity. The result is a wine with polished tannins and a long, peppery finish—no heat, no excess oak, just structure and balance.
